body:
OBSERVED 2026-08-29. The `main protection branch` ruleset (id 15871246) sets

    required_status_checks.strict_required_status_checks_policy = True

which is GitHub's "Require branches to be up to date before merging". Required checks are
validate-author, Fast Tests (Smoke + Unit), Test Suite Summary.

CONSEQUENCE. Roughly ten sessions open PRs against this repo concurrently. Under `strict`, EVERY
merge to main marks EVERY other open PR as BEHIND, and each one must then rebase and re-run the full
required-check set before it can land. The cost per merge is therefore proportional to the number of
open PRs, so aggregate throughput degrades quadratically as concurrency rises, and the PR most likely
to lose is the one with the slowest lane - which is any PR touching the SPA, because it also runs
E2E.

MEASURED THE SAME EVENING:
  * #1956 reported BEHIND three consecutive times before it could land, which is what prompted a
    fleet-wide 25-minute merge freeze.
  * #2019 went BEHIND twice, the second time to a bot commit ("Update translations") that could not
    possibly interact with it semantically. Each occurrence costs a rebase, a force-push and a full
    CI cycle of roughly ten minutes.
  * Two of my PRs additionally reported ci-timeout because pr-lifecycle's wait window is shorter than
    the E2E lane needs, so a slow lane plus a BEHIND compound into repeated resubmission.

This is the deeper cause of the churn that F-4ec664 describes. F-4ec664 is real and worth fixing on
its own - findings/INDEX.md manufactures textual conflicts - but even with that fixed, `strict` alone
guarantees a rebase for every open PR on every merge.

OPTIONS.

  (a) A GitHub MERGE QUEUE. This is precisely the problem merge queues exist for: candidates are
      tested against the projected post-merge main and merged in order, preserving exactly the
      guarantee `strict` provides - that what lands was tested against the main it lands on - without
      making every author rebase serially. Recommended.

  (b) Turn `strict` off. Cheapest, and the repo is not unprotected without it: required checks still
      run, the suite is large, and there is an auto-revert workflow. The residual risk is a semantic
      conflict between two PRs that are individually green - real, but rarer than the cost being paid
      today.

  (c) Keep it and serialise merges by hand. This is the status quo, and it currently means a human
      coordinator calling merge freezes.

⚠️ NOT ACTIONED HERE. Changing branch protection on the operator's repository is a shared-infrastructure
change affecting every session and every contributor, and it is not the sort of thing an individual
session should flip on its own initiative. Filed with the measurement; raised with the dispatcher.
title: main requires branches to be up to date, so every merge invalidates every open PR — throughput degrades quadratically with concurrency
